newsitem.title: FRANCE: Findings of EU Parliament BSE inquiry report.
newsitem.headline: Findings of EU Parliament BSE inquiry report.

text.p: A European Parliament committee of inquiry report, to be voted on Wednesday, strongly attacks Britain and the European Commission for serious errors in the mad cow crisis but stops short of sanctions.

The parliament is also due to vote on Wednesday on a separate resolution which calls on the Commission to take "urgent and effective action" to prevent any recurrence of the public health scare caused by the mad cow epidemic, or face a censure motion.
The resolution differs from another censure motion due on Thursday calling for the immediate dismissal of Commission President Jacques Santer that is expected to be rejected.
Below are the key findings of the report, drafted by Spanish Socialist Euro-MP Manuel Medina Ortega.
Britain and the Commission contest the findings.
The report criticises the European Commission for:
- Giving priority to management of the beef market over protection of public health.
- Downplaying the problem of BSE
- Unclear division of responsibilities for food safety in the Commission's services.
- Failure to carry out BSE inspections in Britain between June 1990 and May 1994
- Failure to regulate suspect meat and bone meal trade across the European market
- Failure to promote an adequate alternative BSE research progamme to British efforts.
- Ignored European Parliament concern over BSE in 1990 and 1993, including a proposal to introduce higher temperatures for the sterilisation of bone meal.
- Exerting political pressure to lift an embargo on British gelatine, semen and tallow exports.
The report attacks the British government, identifying 13 points of alleged negligence over BSE. It says:
- London failed until August 1996 to properly to enforce a ban on exports of animal feed for ruminants which contained meat and bone meal.
- It authorised a change in meat and bone meal production and the system of sterilistion which allowed BSE to emerge.
- It allowed the suspect meal to be exported as cattle feed after it was banned in Britain in 1989.
- It pressured the European Commission to avoid inspecting British slaughterhouses for BSE between 1990-94.
- It tightened this pressure by increasing the presence of its officials and scientific experts on EU advisory committees.
- It did not take scientific evidence and advice seriously.
- It did not honour a promise to EU partners in June 1990 to introduce checks on herds in which BSE had been detected.
- It did not implement legislation under which cattle should have been identified and branded and their movements registered.
- It failed to implement EU rules on veterinary checks by failing to carry out checks on all animal products leaving its territory for the EU market.
- It adopted a blocking policy in the EU in a bid to force the EU to lift an embargo on British beef.
- It did not fully respect the embargo.
- It did not honour an agreement struck with its EU partners at the Florence Summit in June 1996.
- British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg refused to appear before the Parliament's Committee of Inquiry.
- It failed to ensure the proper application of legislation and did not carry out necessary checks.

British officials rejected the report's findings saying it was an "unconvincing and unsubstantiated" summary of British responsibiities and was based on an "absurd and unsubstantiated conspiracy theory."
They totally rejected the suggestion that Britain, under pressure from the meat industry, in turn put pressure on the Commission's veterinary services.
Although animal health controls were not enforced as effectively as they might have been, the officials claimed that Britain now had the strictest and best enforced BSE controls in Europe.
The parliamentary report recommends:
- More openness on BSE and wider publication of research.
- Stricter monitoring to enforce the bans on British beef and suspect animal feed.
- Reform of the Commission's human and animal health services and new legal powers for the Commission in these areas.
A public health protection unit, covering both human and animal health, should be created to coordinate efforts free from pressure of agricultural or industrial interests.
- Britain to eradicate BSE and to submit selective cull programme to the Commission as soon as possible.
- Introduce an independent EU research programme into BSE.
- EU rules to enforce highest animal feed standrds with clear labelling on ingredients.
- Individual animal identification or "passports."
- Commission to propose compensation for new victims of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, the human equivalent of BSE.
